title: Why is household electricity uptake low in Sub-Saharan Africa?
citation: With Moussa P. Blimpo and Agnieszka Postepska · World Development, 133 (2020).
summary: Using harmonized household surveys across more than 30 Sub-Saharan African countries and qualitative fieldwork, we find that demand-side constraints account for more than two-fifths of the electricity access deficit. Income, housing quality, and community infrastructure shape adoption, highlighting the importance of complementary policies alongside grid expansion.
authors: Moussa P. Blimpo, Agnieszka Postepska, and Yanbin Xu

title: Technology in the Classroom and Learning in Secondary Schools
citation: With Moussa P. Blimpo, Ousman Gajigo, Solomon Owusu, and Ryoko Tomita · World Bank Policy Research Working Paper No. 9288 (2020).
summary: We evaluate computer-assisted learning in secondary schools in The Gambia using administrative and survey data. The program increased mathematics certification scores by 0.59 standard deviations and the share of students obtaining credit by 15 percentage points, providing evidence on technology-enabled instruction in a low-income setting.
authors: Moussa P. Blimpo, Ousman Gajigo, Solomon Owusu, Ryoko Tomita, and Yanbin Xu

title: From Market Opening to Innovation: Effective Contestability in Digital Markets
summary: When does market opening produce an innovative competitor? A two-period stochastic general-equilibrium model separates the thresholds for rival entry and innovation. In the EU iOS app-distribution calibration, observed access supports entry, but benchmark rival innovation remains unprofitable even at full access. Stronger inherited quality and productivity or greater innovation capacity can bring innovation within reach. Platform R&D and welfare can rise even as platform profits fall.

figure.alt: Entry and innovation thresholds fall as inherited rival quality and productivity gaps close. At 22.62% gap closure, the innovation threshold reaches observed access of 0.47.
figure.caption: Figure 7, September 2026 draft: entry and innovation regimes along the less-disadvantaged rival path. Closing 22.62% of each inherited quality and productivity gap brings the innovation threshold to observed effective access (κ = 0.47). Slightly greater gap closure supports positive rival innovation. Source: paper, p. 44 .

title: Beyond Market Concentration: Measuring Contestability in Digital Markets
citation: With Zhiyang Cheng and Amr Yakout · Working paper, July 2026.
summary: We measure competitive opportunity across four channels: user mobility, rival access and distribution, platform neutrality, and access to data, interoperability, and infrastructure. Distinguishing formal legal protections from opportunities realized in practice, the framework covers nine jurisdictions and pilot applications to search and mobile app distribution. The results reveal gaps between legal opening and effective challenge, with different barriers across markets.

title: Comments on the First Review of the Digital Markets Act
citation: Yale Tobin Center for Economic Policy · Policy research, 2026.
summary: An assessment of early DMA implementation, focusing on contestability, compliance, and innovation incentives. The analysis connects enforcement challenges to market access, entry conditions, and the distribution of platform rents.
authors: Fiona Scott Morton, Alissa Cooper, Jacques Crémer, Amelia Fletcher, Paul Heidhues, Giorgio Monti, Rupprecht Podszun, Alexandre de Streel, and Tracy Xu

title: Designing the Technical Committee for the United States v. Google Search Antitrust Remedy: A Blueprint for Effective Implementation
summary: This report proposes an institutional design for overseeing remedy implementation in United States v. Google LLC. Drawing on the Microsoft remedy and recent regulatory experience, it sets out technical access, authority, and monitoring procedures to address information asymmetries and support effective enforcement.
authors: Contributors: Zander Arnao, Felix Chen, Alissa Cooper, Timothy Cowen, Joseph Jerome, Michael Kraver, Karina Montoya, Tracy Xu, and Sophia Yakhno

title: Internal Migration Restrictions, Aggregate Productivity, and Spatial Growth
summary: A dynamic spatial general-equilibrium model quantifies how China’s hukou restrictions shape labor allocation and aggregate productivity. The framework incorporates trade, agglomeration, endogenous amenities, and migration costs by registration status. Counterfactual reforms examine regional inequality and long-run spatial growth.

title: High-Speed Rail: Impacts on Mobility Costs and Spatial Reallocation
summary: This project extends my spatial framework to study how reductions in transportation costs interact with institutional migration frictions. It examines how high-speed rail changes regional specialization, labor allocation, and productivity—and how those effects depend on the migration regime.

title: Digital Skills and Labor Market Demand in Central Asia
summary: This project examines how digital competencies relate to employment, wage premia, and skills mismatch in Central Asia, using employer surveys, wage data, and skills assessments.

title: Digital Skills for Lifelong Learning (DS4LL), Kyrgyzstan
summary: An impact evaluation of digital skills training and competency development across approximately 300 secondary schools in Kyrgyzstan. The project combines student and teacher assessments with implementation data to study learning and institutional capacity.

title: The Economics of Artificial Intelligence: Market Structure, Innovation, and Welfare
summary: Developing economic frameworks to study how AI market structure, access to key inputs, and firms’ capabilities affect competition, innovation incentives, and welfare.
